The kingdom now, consummated at his coming
Amillennial
The right view
Daniel 7 is an ascension scene: the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives the kingdom. Psalm 110 and Peter place the enthronement at the ascension.
The church is Zion, Jerusalem and the temple
The apostles call the church the Jerusalem above, Mount Zion, God’s temple and the bride. Jesus said his kingdom is not from this world, and is among you.
The thousand years is now
Symbolic and present: Satan is bound from deceiving the nations, and the saints reign with Christ as his body, he the head.
The new creation has begun
The new heavens and earth began with the new covenant and grow to fullness. The Spirit and the bride say “come” now.
One coming brings the end
At his coming: the resurrection, immortality, one judgement, death destroyed as the last enemy, and the kingdom handed to the Father.
The age that ended was the old covenant
AD 30-70 was an overlap of the two covenants. Many “coming” texts are judgement-comings in the Old Testament pattern.
Ascension
Christ enthroned; the kingdom inaugurated.
Transition
The old covenant vanishing; the end of the age; judgement on old Jerusalem.
The gospel age: the thousand years
Satan bound as to the nations; the church is Zion, temple and bride, reigning with Christ. Death being defeated, the new creation advancing.
The last trumpet: one resurrection and immortality, one judgement.
Eternity
Handover and fullness
Death, the last enemy, destroyed; the kingdom given to the Father; no more tears.
Second coming
A thousand-year reign: mortals and glorified together

Reign now
Enthroned at the ascension; the saints share the reign as the body under the head.
Enemies under his feet
He reigns until his enemies are subdued; the body obeys the head and brings subjection through the gospel. Death is last.
Not an earthly fantasy
The kingdom is righteousness, peace and joy. The disciples did not fight, because it is not worldly in source or method.
Zion and temple
Jesus never pointed to a rebuilt city or temple; the apostles apply both to the church.
The transition
The old and new covenants overlapped until AD 70; Hebrews speaks into that moment.
Bound as to deceiving the nations, yet still active in individual minds, as sin and death are defeated yet not believed by all.
Progress to no more tears
Revelation 21-22 holds an open invitation: the gates stay open and the nations are healed. The new creation is advancing now.
Isaiah 65:20
A gospel-age picture: the curse being reversed and early death shrinking, until the final resurrection; Revelation 21:4 shows completion.
The gospel goes out; then the resurrection at his coming brings fullness.
One resurrection, one judgement
Jesus speaks of a single hour and a single last day.
The handover
He reigns until the end, then delivers the kingdom to the Father.
Mortals and immortals together
Those of the age to come cannot die any more. A world of glorified saints beside dying nations mixes the two ages.
Death after the resurrection
Death is swallowed up when we are changed at the last trumpet; premillennialism leaves death at work for a thousand years afterwards.
Two “last days”
Jesus raises believers on the last day, and gives one hour for both groups.
A deferred throne
Peter ties David’s throne to the resurrection and ascension; James sees David’s tent rebuilt now.
Time texts pushed away
“Soon”, “near”, “this generation”. Daniel was told to seal his book; John is told not to.
A restored temple
Hebrews says there is no more offering for sin, yet Ezekiel’s sacrifices “make atonement”.
All of Matthew 24 as the final coming
“This generation” in Matthew means Jesus’ contemporaries.
Every coming merged into one
Old Testament cloud-comings were judgements in history. Not every coming must be the last.
A binding with no visible effect
If the strong man is bound and plundered, the nations should be discipled, not described mainly by decline.
Revelation 21-22 only as the eternal state
The invitation “come” and the healing of the nations are present-age activities inside the final vision.
A stone that fills the earth
Daniel 2 describes growth, not only a sudden end; a pessimistic reading struggles with that growth.
Revelation 19 as the end, yet “soon”
Reading the fall of Babylon as future collides with the time statements of chapters 1 and 22.
If glorified saints cannot die, how do they live for a thousand years beside mortals who do?
Jesus lived among his disciples after his resurrection, so immortal and mortal can coexist.
That was forty days, not a governed age. And where does Paul say death is destroyed after a thousand more years of dying, when it is swallowed up at the resurrection?
Paul says “then comes the end” after his coming. Where does the text place a thousand-year gap?
“Then” allows an interval, and Revelation 20 supplies it.
An allowed gap is not a stated one. Christ reigns until the last enemy falls, and it falls at the resurrection. Where is the reign after that?
Peter says Jesus now sits on David’s throne. Why defer it?
Revelation 3:21 distinguishes the Father’s throne from Christ’s own; David’s throne is future.
Peter links the promise to the resurrection and Psalm 110, and James says David’s tent is being rebuilt. Which apostle says the throne is still waiting?
Hebrews says the old sacrifices could never take away sins. Why would Ezekiel’s sacrifices return?
They are memorials, as the Lord’s Supper looks back.
Ezekiel says they make atonement. Why use atonement language for a memorial, and why return to shadows after the reality has come?
Jesus gives one “hour” for both resurrections. Why two phases a thousand years apart?
Revelation 20:4-6 distinguishes a first and a second resurrection.
Revelation 20:4 speaks of souls who lived; Jesus and Paul speak of one last day and one resurrection of just and unjust. Why not read Revelation 20 in their light?
Revelation’s events must “soon” take place. How long is soon for the seven churches?
It means suddenly, or swiftly once it begins.
Revelation 22:10 contrasts Daniel’s sealed vision with John’s unsealed one because the time is near. A far future empties the contrast.
The New Testament calls the church Zion, temple, Jerusalem and bride. Where does it tell us to await a physical city or temple?
Luke 21:24 and Romans 11:26 keep a future for Israel.
Luke 21:24 sits inside an AD 70 context, and Paul calls the church the Israel of God and one olive tree. Which text commands us to expect a rebuilt temple?
If the whole of Matthew 24 is the final return, which generation is “this generation”?
The Jewish people, or a kind of people, not a time span.
Matthew uses it for Jesus’ contemporaries elsewhere. Why would 24:34 change meaning without a signal?
If every coming is the final one, what of Old Testament cloud-comings?
Those are types; the New Testament uses them for the final coming.
Then the pattern is granted: God comes in historical judgement. Where does Matthew 24 mark the switch from AD 70 to the end?
Satan is bound now. Why expect steady decline?
The binding is limited, and the church suffers until the end.
The strong man’s house is plundered and Christ has all authority. What does a bound enemy and a discipling church look like, if not progress?
Revelation 22:17 invites people to come, inside the final vision. If chapters 21-22 are only the eternal state, who is invited?
Present readers are addressed inside a vision of the future.
Then the chapters blend present and final. Why not accept that the new creation is already advancing?
The stone grows into a mountain that fills the earth. Is that growth, or only an instant at the end?
The stone strikes at the end and the kingdom is eternal.
Daniel says it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth. Where is the growth in a view that expects the world mostly to resist?
Revelation 19 and 22 say these events are soon. Why read them as future?
The language symbolises the whole church age and applies throughout.
If it applies throughout, the time statements mean little. A first-century fall of Babylon keeps them meaningful.
The olive tree is one tree. Where in Romans 11 is a separate Jewish programme, land or temple?
The tree is Israel’s covenants; Gentiles are added, and Israel’s national future is still ahead.
Paul speaks of branches entering by faith and grafted back by faith. Which verse names land, temple or throne rather than mercy and faith?
If “all Israel” means the nation at the end, why does Paul say not all Israel is Israel?
That is about the remnant now; “all Israel” in chapter 11 is the national turning.
Then Paul uses “Israel” in two senses within three chapters. What in 11:26 marks the switch, and why is Galatians 6:16 not a third?
Paul quotes Isaiah 59 and Jeremiah 31 for the Deliverer and the covenant. Why not a first-coming fulfilment?
Paul says “will come”, so it is future, at his return.
Jeremiah 31 is the new covenant that Hebrews says is already in force. Why would it need a later Jewish fulfilment?
What would it take for “and so” to mean “and then”?
The “until” in verse 25 gives it a time sense.
The lexicons give manner as the main sense, and the verses before describe a process: jealousy and grafting. Is the time reading carrying more than the Greek bears?
Paul redefines Israel
Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel; the true Jew is inward; the church is the Israel of God and the circumcision.
One tree, entered by faith
Branches stand by faith. Gentiles do not replace Israel; they join the commonwealth of Israel.
“And so” means “in this way”
Gentile inclusion makes Israel jealous, and Jews are saved the same way, by faith, as the fullness of the Gentiles comes in.
The covenant quoted is the new covenant
Isaiah 59 and Jeremiah 31 are already inaugurated, as Hebrews says.
No land, temple or throne
Romans 9-11 never mentions them. Abraham’s promise was to inherit the world, and the aim is mercy to all.
In 11:25-26 “Israel” is set against “the Gentiles”, so it means the nation.
Paul contrasts hardened Israel with the Gentiles to show who is being added. Unbelieving Jews are grafted back only by faith. The contrast is about status, not two programmes.
“Their fullness” and “their acceptance” are ethnic.
Yes, and the postmillennial version accepts a large Jewish turning. That is still gospel-age conversion, with no land or temple.
“Beloved for the sake of the fathers.”
God keeps covenant faithfulness to Abraham’s seed through Jews who believe in every generation. The gifts are irrevocable because the promise stands in Christ.
